clue.text: One out, perhaps, to disrupt entertainment, being devious?

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase: devious, meaning roundabout

indicators.note: to disrupt something is to break into it, so one piece is pushed inside the other

parts.note: a circus is a travelling show, a kind of entertainment
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of out may come in another arrangement

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone who drops out to wreck a show is being underhand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns OUT into TOU, and 'to disrupt' puts I plus TOU inside CIRCUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Devious can mean winding or indirect in route, which is a synonym of roundabout.

clue.text: Norse deity encountered in head armour

parts.note: Hel is the Norse goddess of the underworld
met means encountered

explanation.surface: A Viking god turns up wearing a war helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: A protective covering worn on the head in battle is exactly what this piece of armour is.

clue.text: Canon making stink about cultural pursuits?

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so one word goes around the other

parts.note: pong is British slang for a stink
the arts are cultural pursuits

explanation.surface: A churchman raises a stink over arty activities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canon' looks like a clergyman; here it is the musical canon, a round. 'about' puts PONG around ARTS. PONG is everyday British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is a piece in which voices sing the same melody staggered, one type of vocal piece for several singers.

clue.text: Source of steam? British tanker

parts.note: an oiler is a ship that carries oil, a tanker

explanation.surface: Asking whether a British oil tanker is what is giving off steam.
explanation.definitionFit: Water is heated in this vessel to make steam for heating or engines.

clue.text: Drink, roughly a quid — take one

indicators.note: roughly suggests the letters of a quid are handled carelessly and rearranged

parts.note: the fodder as the setter needed it, with a second I
R, from Latin recipe, is the abbreviation for take on prescriptions
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A cocktail costing about a pound: have one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' rearranges A QUID, but the answer needs a second I the clue does not supply: the setter's slip. A quid is British slang for one pound sterling.
explanation.definitionFit: This rum cocktail with lime and sugar is a mixed drink.

clue.text: Note very good average

parts.note: so (or soh) is the fifth note of the sol-fa scale
so means very, as in so good

explanation.surface: A remark that a very good grade is only average.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good' joins the pieces to the definition here; the second SO is 'very'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something middling, neither good nor bad, is merely mediocre.

clue.text: Enthusiasm for shoot

explanation.surface: Keenness for going shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire means passion or ardour, and to fire a gun is to discharge it.

clue.text: Old English, a new lip cosmetic mostly put on after a kiss

indicators.note: after places the following piece behind the kiss
mostly means not quite all, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: lip gloss is a shiny lip cosmetic
X is the conventional written kiss
a play that is put on is said to be on

explanation.surface: Applying most of a fresh lip product right after a kiss, in old-fashioned terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims GLOSS to GLOS; 'after' puts ON behind A and X.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglo-Saxon is the name for the earliest form of the English language, before the Norman Conquest.

clue.text: Cultivate lots of politicians, perhaps, at these gatherings?

parts.note: to garden is to cultivate land
political parties are groups of politicians

explanation.surface: Advice to court politicians at social events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cultivate' reads as courting people; it is tending soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Outdoor social receptions held on a lawn are a kind of formal gathering.

clue.text: A formidable weapon, it plays a part in reduction of racism

indicators.note: playing a part in something means being inside it, so one piece sits within the other
reduction here means breaking down, so the letters of racism are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A dangerous weapon has a role in cutting down prejudice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduction of' rearranges RACISM to SCIMAR; 'plays a part in' puts IT inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved oriental sword with a single edge is a fearsome blade.

clue.text: Sound of someone lapping up drink

indicators.note: sound of tells us the word is heard rather than written

parts.note: one who laps something up with the tongue is a licker

explanation.surface: The noise of an animal lapping up a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquor means alcoholic spirits, strong drink.

clue.text: Writer crossing street to get to restaurant

indicators.note: crossing here means going across and enclosing, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: a Biro is a ballpoint pen, a writer

explanation.surface: An author crossing the road to reach a café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests an author; it is a pen. 'crossing' puts BIRO around ST. Biro is the British everyday name for a ballpoint pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A bistro is a small informal restaurant.

clue.text: Problems with grannie's income

indicators.note: problems suggests the letters are in trouble and get jumbled

parts.note: the possessive here supplies its S as a letter

explanation.surface: Grandma's income has difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the 's of grannie's is a letter: GRANNIES rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Money earned from work is a person's wages or revenue.

clue.text: He usually has the lead in a western

definitions.text: He usually has the lead in a western

parts.words: He usually has the lead in a western
parts.note: the lead is not the starring role but the bullets fired by a gun-toting cowboy

explanation.surface: Who normally stars in a cowboy film?
explanation.definitionFit: A gunfighter of the Wild West is the stock character shooting bullets in such films.

clue.text: Ready for retirement?

parts.note: ready is slang for money, so this means cash paid to someone who has retired

explanation.surface: Asking if someone is prepared to stop working.
explanation.definitionFit: The state payment made to older people after they stop work is retirement money.

clue.text: Potions to help us sleep through board meetings?

explanation.surface: Sleeping draughts handed round to get through dull board meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads as company meetings; it is games played on a board. Draughts is the British name for checkers.
explanation.definitionFit: A draught is a dose of medicine to drink, and draughts is the board game called checkers in the US.

clue.text: Authoress madly in love? Hush!

indicators.note: madly suggests the letters of in love go wild and rearrange

parts.note: taken as written
st is an exclamation calling for quiet

explanation.surface: A woman writer is crazily in love but told to be quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A female writer of fiction is one kind of author of books.

clue.text: Fallen pear lies by fruit tree

indicators.note: fallen suggests the letters tumble down and land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pear that has dropped lies beside the tree it came from.
explanation.definitionFit: An espalier is a fruit tree trained to grow flat against a wall or frame.

clue.text: Type of ink used for Independent and Scotsman?

parts.note: Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: Which ink is used to print two newspapers, the Independent and the Scotsman?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface names two newspapers; one is an abbreviation and the other a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Indian ink is a dense black drawing ink.

clue.text: Base broken into by Irish male in a very robust way?

definitions.text: male in a very robust way?

indicators.note: broken into by puts the following piece inside the first

parts.note: base means low and vile

explanation.surface: Something low is burgled by an Irishman who is very strong.
explanation.definitionFit: Virile describes manly vigour and strength, robust masculinity.

clue.text: Discover doctor's broken regulation

indicators.note: the doctor has broken the regulation, so the doctor's letters go inside it

parts.note: a rule is a regulation
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, stands for doctor; the 's means has

explanation.surface: Finding out that a doctor has breached the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: To rumble someone is British slang for finding out what they are up to.
explanation.definitionFit: To rumble a scheme is to see through it, to find it out.

clue.text: Suggest age difference not fully represented

indicators.note: not fully signals that only a run from within these words is used

explanation.surface: Proposing that an age gap was only partly portrayed.
explanation.definitionFit: A play staged is put on or presented to an audience.

clue.text: Run made by man on left wing

explanation.surface: A run made by a left-wing activist.
explanation.definitionFit: To trot is to run at a jog, and a Trot is a Trotskyist, a far-left radical.

clue.text: Light that is taken around in Mull, perhaps

indicators.note: taken around means these letters are wrapped about the other piece

parts.note: ie, id est, means that is

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters of in Mull may come in another order

explanation.surface: Lighting being carried round the Scottish island of Mull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IN MULL to LLUMIN; 'taken around' wraps IE about it. Mull is an island in western Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: To illumine is to light up, a literary verb.

clue.text: Things found in Oxford, outside Union -missing luggage?

indicators.note: outside means one piece is wrapped about the other

parts.note: lost cases are suitcases gone missing

explanation.surface: Items turning up in Oxford outside the Union building after bags went astray.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford was called by Matthew Arnold the home of lost causes; the Oxford Union is the university debating society.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford is famously the home of hopeless crusades, doomed efforts.

clue.text: Staffordshire town provided most of university's backing

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters are read in reverse
most of means not quite all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: Keele is a university in Staffordshire

explanation.surface: A town that supplied the bulk of a university's financial support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims KEELE to KEEL; 'backing' turns it round. Staffordshire is an English county in the Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Leek is a market town in north Staffordshire, England.
